title: Living with chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia alongside cataract, peptic ulcer disease, diabetes and hypertension in Ghana
case_prompt:
A 51-year-old Ghanaian woman with a history of hypertension since age 32 and type II diabetes mellitus since age 34 presented for evaluation of bilateral eyelid drooping. She first noticed left upper-eyelid ptosis at age 17, which gradually worsened and was followed by right-sided ptosis. Over the following years, she developed progressive limitation of all extraocular movements but had normal pupillary reactions and no nystagmus. She denied diplopia, ocular pain, diurnal variation, exercise intolerance, dysphagia, or other muscle weakness.

Myasthenia gravis was considered but an ice-pack test was negative and her exam remained consistent on multiple visits. There was no family history of similar ocular disease. 

In 2020, visual acuity was 6/12+3 in the right eye and 6/9+3 in the left; intraocular pressures were elevated at 39 mmHg OD and 41 mmHg OS with normal cup-to-disc ratios. She was diagnosed with ocular hypertension and started on timolol drops. Fundoscopy was unremarkable. In 2021, progressive lens opacity led to visual acuity decline to 6/36 OD and 6/18 OS; she underwent bilateral small-incision cataract extraction, after which acuity improved to 6/18 OD and 6/12 OS and intraocular pressures fell to 21 mmHg and 20 mmHg on timolol. She declined ptosis surgery and laser trabeculoplasty.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Myasthenia gravis — “Myasthenia gravis was ruled out by an ice‐pack test and also clinically, as the patient presented many times to the eye clinic exactly the same way.”  
2. Ocular myositis — “There was no ocular pain; therefore, ocular myositis was ruled out.”  
3. Tolosa–Hunt syndrome — “Tolsa‐Hunt syndrome was also ruled out due to the lack of suggestive symptoms. Severe periorbital headaches, painful eye movements (ophthalmoplegia), and ophthalmoparesis are also present in this syndrome.”  
4. CPEO-plus — “CPEO‐plus was ruled out because other neurological symptoms associated with the syndrome were absent.”  
5. Kearns–Sayre syndrome — “Kearns–Sayre syndrome (KSS) can be ruled out because … pigmentary retinopathy, cerebellar ataxia, heart block, and/or elevated cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) protein >100 mg/dL (the triad) were not present.”
